title: Probability & Bayesian Inference
description: Study conditional probability and bayes' rule, expectation, variance and covariance, maximum likelihood and map, and posterior predictive uncertainty. Each lesson includes a worked example and an applied practice task.

lessons.title: Conditional probability and Bayes' rule
lessons.description: Compute the approximate probability of the condition given a positive result.
lessons.conceptOverview: Bayes' rule combines likelihood with prior probability and normalizes by the evidence. Rare-event base rates can dominate the interpretation of a positive test even when sensitivity is high.
lessons.whyItMatters: Posterior probability depends on prevalence as well as test accuracy.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: In 10000 cases with 1 percent prevalence, a test with 90 percent sensitivity and 5 percent false-positive rate yields about 90 true positives and 495 false positives.

sections.title: Practice & verification
sections.content: Compute the approximate probability of the condition given a positive result. Write down your reasoning and check it against the concept before continuing.

keyTakeaways: Posterior probability depends on prevalence as well as test accuracy.
commonMistakes: A 90 percent sensitive test implies a 90 percent posterior for every positive.

lessons.title: Expectation, variance and covariance
lessons.description: Calculate the variance if covariance is negative 0.5 instead.
lessons.conceptOverview: Expectation is linear without requiring independence. Variance of a sum includes covariance terms; ignoring them underestimates or overestimates uncertainty when variables are correlated.
lessons.whyItMatters: Variance aggregation must account for covariance.
lessons.engineerDeepDive: Expectation is linear without requiring independence. Variance of a sum includes covariance terms; ignoring them underestimates or overestimates uncertainty when variables are correlated.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Expectation is linear without requiring independence. Variance of a sum includes covariance terms; ignoring them underestimates or overestimates uncertainty when variables are correlated.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Two measurements each have variance 1 and covariance 0.5, giving their sum variance 3.

sections.title: Practice & verification
sections.content: Calculate the variance if covariance is negative 0.5 instead. Write down your reasoning and check it against the concept before continuing.

keyTakeaways: Variance aggregation must account for covariance.
commonMistakes: The variance of a sum is always the sum of variances.

lessons.title: Maximum likelihood and MAP
lessons.description: Explain how stronger prior precision changes the preferred weights.
lessons.conceptOverview: Maximum likelihood maximizes data likelihood; maximum a posteriori also incorporates a prior. A prior can act like regularization, but its effect depends on parameterization and strength.
lessons.whyItMatters: MAP combines data fit with a prior contribution.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Maximum likelihood maximizes data likelihood; maximum a posteriori also incorporates a prior. A prior can act like regularization, but its effect depends on parameterization and strength.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A Gaussian prior on regression weights adds a squared-weight penalty to the negative log-likelihood objective.

sections.title: Practice & verification
sections.content: Explain how stronger prior precision changes the preferred weights. Write down your reasoning and check it against the concept before continuing.

keyTakeaways: MAP combines data fit with a prior contribution.
commonMistakes: MAP and maximum likelihood are always identical.

lessons.title: Posterior predictive uncertainty
lessons.description: Separate parameter uncertainty, noise and model mismatch in this example.
lessons.conceptOverview: Predictive uncertainty integrates uncertainty about parameters with observation noise under the model. A narrow estimate can still be wrong if the model is misspecified or evaluated far outside its support.
lessons.whyItMatters: Model assumptions limit the interpretation of predictive uncertainty.
